rv.q: The end result is certainly the funniest show on Broadway in years, if not the most likable.
He’s the cream in the borscht, the schmaltz in the gribenes, and his prodigious charm makes Mr. Saturday Night a very haimish experience.
So why did I enjoy it so much? When the show isn't trying to be a musical, it puts Crystal up in front of us and has him do Buddy's act.

You’ll be relieved to know Billy Crystal is still a stand-up guy — stand-up in the sense that the jokes in 'Mr. Saturday Night,' the 1992 film comedy he and other showbiz pros have turned into a slender but agreeable Broadway musical — are old-school funny, polished and impeccably timed.
Crystal's performance is the show's main draw, and he delivers with the easy authority of a seasoned entertainer who knows how to work a room.

There's one thing to kvetch about with "Mr. Saturday Night": it would be better as a straight play than a song-and-dance show. Jason Robert Brown has composed a bland point-A-to-point-B score that's not as hilarious or textured as the text. Similar to "Tootsie" before it, the star here is the scenes, not the tunes.
And if you’re in search of hilarity, retro good times and Crystal’s now-precious signature smoothie of affirmation, timing and stark comedic honesty, “Mr. Saturday Night” is your show.
The structure of the musical is nicely roomy, giving Crystal ample time to perform standup, sell jokes, and serve up his shtick. It works!
As a piece of theater, the show is a bit of a mess; the jokes, even some of the hoary ones, work better than the storytelling, and the acting styles are all over the place.
But there is precious little pulse throughout “Mr. Saturday Night,” a double shot at redemption for both Buddy and his marquee creator.

The cast does its damndest. Paymer and Crystal exude palpable brotherly warmth. Graff is the show's most valuable player, her comedic delivery almost upstaging Crystal. Bean sings the bejeezus out of her ballads.
Mr. Saturday Night is filled with joy: Crystal's joy of performing for us (the one-liners crackle and gleam), and our joy in watching the performances.
If you love Billy Crystal, book a ticket. He's funny, charming, not grandstanding.
The chemistry between the brothers – or, more accurately, between real-life pals and long-ago co-stars Crystal and Paymer – is easily the most enjoyable thing in a generally enjoyable production.
But for those looking for a Broadway show that's livelier than a Catskills performance, you might have a hard time finding it.
There's something engaging about each of these three basic layers of 'Mr. Saturday Night,' although Crystal's comedy far more so than the story or the music.
He’s so assured—in the perhaps forgotten manner of George Burns and George Jessel—he compensates sufficiently to make himself Mr. Every Night of the Week.
But there’s nothing about the musical that displays a reason for being, other than to showcase its star’s extraordinary comic chops.

But along with the rest of the creative team, including director John Rando (Urinetown), who guides the less-than-deluxe-looking production, the songwriters haven't presented a compelling argument that Buddy's story expands as a musical.

While Crystal and the cast are droll and endearing, “Mr. Saturday Night” (directed by John Rando with an especially small cast for an old-fashioned-style musical comedy) is pretty dull, slow, and schmaltzy.
At its heart, the musical “Mr. Saturday Night” is as sentimental as it is dishonest.
Crystal delivers the kind of star performance that has been mostly missing from Broadway this season and which audiences are eating up with a giant teaspoon.
The sometimes schmaltzy book and characters are undeniably old-fashioned, geared to traditional old-time Broadway audiences.

Unsure about seeing Mr. Saturday Night? Take this simple quiz. Do you enjoy watching Billy Crystal do what he does better than anybody, weaponizing punchlines and detonating them for explosive laughs? Head to the Nederlander now.
However, anyone else may find this decent show to be a tired affair which just about sustains its two-and-half-hour running time.
Unfortunately the show has limited audience appeal and I can’t see a younger audience enjoying this the way their parents and grandparents would.

So while there are the occasional bursts of brilliance, as in Graff singing “Tahiti” while in a daydream, unfortunately, as a whole there isn’t quite the musical comedy magic we’d expect from a collaboration between veteran composers like Brown and stars like Crystal, Paymer, and Graff.
